claim: In a truly random, unbiased sample of YouTube videos (not gated by popularity, channel size, or subscriber threshold), only 0.21% showed both coders agreeing that visible monetization (sponsorship, promotion, or advertising beyond YouTube's own ads) was present, rising to at most 2.98% if either coder flagged it.
stance_target: Registration/upload counts used as denominators for creator living-wage-share statistics massively overstate the population that ever attempted to monetize, so the living-wage share among genuine occupational attempts is materially higher than sub-2% telemetry-based estimates suggest
scope_conditions: n=1,000 randomly selected videos (989 usable after discarding 11 coding errors) hand-coded by 14 coders in November 2022, drawn from a larger random sample of 10,016 videos collected via a novel brute-force video-ID sampling method ('Dialing for Videos') that avoids recommendation-algorithm and channel-threshold biases; global sample by construction, not restricted to English/Western content at the sampling stage; Krippendorff's alpha for the monetization question was only 0.12, reflecting genuine rarity/ambiguity of the signal rather than measurement noise inflating the estimate
quoted_support: Coders only agreed that monetization was present 0.21% of the time, with at least one person indicating there was monetization an additional 2.77% of the time... Both of these questions had very low reliability scores (monetization α = 0.12...)
region: Global (random video-ID sampling, not geography-restricted at the sampling stage)

claim: The authors conclude directly that most YouTube content is not an attempt at the 'creator economy' at all: 'questions...about how often they [creators] monetize their videos -- are simply not applicable to most videos in a sample like this.'
stance_target: The overwhelming majority of registered/uploaded YouTube activity is not an occupational attempt, so denominators built from total channel or video counts are not measuring 'people who tried to make a living from content creation'
scope_conditions: Authors' own interpretive conclusion, drawn from the same n=1,000 hand-coded random sample and n=10,016 metadata sample
quoted_support: Rather than finding evidence that most YouTube users wanted to be part of a creator economy, we found surprising and unusual uses for the platform... questions...about how often they monetize their videos - are simply not applicable to most videos in a sample like this.

claim: In this random video-level sample, the median subscriber count of the posting channel was just 4, versus a mean of 55,100 -- a channel population several orders of magnitude below the 1,000-subscriber floor every YouTube income-telemetry study in this corpus uses as its denominator.
stance_target: The true base-rate 'YouTube channel' is a near-zero-audience entity, not a person pursuing content creation as an occupation, reinforcing that raw channel-count denominators inflate the apparent occupational-failure rate
scope_conditions: n=10,016 randomly sampled videos, late 2022; subscriber count is of the channel that posted the sampled video, so this is video-weighted, not channel-weighted, but is the least popularity-biased channel-subscriber statistic available for YouTube as a whole

claim: Extrapolating from the random sample, YouTube hosted an estimated 9,881,141,822 (~9.88 billion) publicly visible videos as of late 2022, of which 46.20% were uploaded in just the final two years (2021-2022), indicating recent explosive growth in low-scrutiny content that pre-dates most academic creator-economy studies' sampling windows.
stance_target: Establishing the overall scale and growth rate of YouTube's content base as context for any denominator claim
scope_conditions: Estimate derived from the random video-ID sampling method's known ID-space coverage; excludes private and unlisted videos, so this is a floor estimate, not a ceiling
quoted_support: Extrapolating from our sampling methods, we can offer an estimate of the size of YouTube (9,881,141,822 publicly searchable videos at the time of our late-2022 sampling window), a growth curve for the number of videos hosted by the site (46.20% uploaded in 2021 and 2022)

claim: In the random video sample, 86.93% of videos had fewer than 1,000 views and 4.88% had never been watched at all (zero views), with mean views (5,868) nearly 170 times the median (35).
stance_target: Extreme right-skew and a large near-zero-attention floor characterize YouTube as a whole, not just its income distribution
scope_conditions: n=10,016 randomly sampled videos, late 2022; public/listed videos only
quoted_support: The vast majority of YouTube videos (86.93%) are seen by fewer than 1,000 people. A significant number (4.88%) are never watched at all

claim: Only 20.1% of sampled YouTube video audio was detected as English, with Hindi (7.6%), Spanish (6.2%) and Russian (4.2%) the next largest, showing that the English-language, Western-centric datasets underlying most academic creator-income literature (e.g. the YouNiverse/Hua et al. dataset) describe a small minority of the platform.
stance_target: English-language academic creator-economy datasets are broadly representative of YouTube as a whole
scope_conditions: Language detected via an automated audio-language-ID pipeline on the n=10,016 random sample; authors caution the language model likely misidentifies some videos, so exact percentages should be read as approximate, though the ordering and English-minority finding is robust
quoted_support: Only 20.1% of YouTube videos were in English, 7.6% were in Hindi, 6.2% were in Spanish, and 4.2% were in Russian
region: Global -- directly cautions against generalizing Western/English-language creator-economy findings, relevant to the Southeast Asia flag
